Art and Media in a Digital Society
Caution: this information is subject to change

By the end of this course, students should be able to:

Knowledge:  
  • K1: Define key concepts and important themes within the fields of media and cultural studies;
  • K2: Explain how these concepts and histories shape digitalization and the relations between offline and online media;
  • K3: Apply research methods of media and cultural studies to interpret how forms of media and art interact to produce meaning;
Skills:  
  • S1: Interpret various art forms across different media (e.g., film, literature, music, etc.);
  • S2: Defend their ideas in writing and verbally for specific audiences;
  • S3: Evaluate the effectiveness of argumentation and analysis in academic writing and scientific methods, as well as genres intended for a broader audience, such as journalism;
Character:  
  • C1: Organize their ideas in relation to the multiple perspectives of their peers and primary and secondary sources;  
  • C2: Formulate their ideas verbally and in writing to reason and argue respectfully in the process of learning, even when dissensus arises.

<body>In this course we will investigate the relations between media and culture, as well as relations among art, social movements and issues, and other domains of life. What influences from the visual arts can we find in fiction or poetry? How can music influence painting or literature? What can films do that novels can’t (and vice versa)? How do different media enhance or counteract each other, for instance, at a festival? How does art relate to everyday life, and what is art to begin with? How can art meaningfully relate to societal and cultural issues? As everything becomes intermedial and digital, what does that mean for art, culture, and society? To answer these questions, we will begin by exploring artistic and intellectual histories of the twentieth and twenty-first century before moving on to how these histories apply to cultural contexts and production today. These sessions will deepen and expand understandings of the core concepts of this course, including intermediality, transmediality, multimediality, performance, medium specificity, and remediation. In the final four sessions, we will apply the foundational knowledge and skills we developed in the first eight sessions of the course. We will place all these interrelations in the broader cultural frame of the networked society, interdisciplinarity, and thinking in terms of ‘difference’ and ‘relating’. By the end of this course, students will have the knowledge and skills they need to be engaged interlocutors in cultural, artistic, and digital trends that shape ideas, politics, and worldviews.</body>
